subject: mathematics
question_text: If A, B, C are angles of a triangle, then prove that sin²(A/2) + sin²(B/2) + sin²(C/2) = 1 − 2 sin(A/2) sin(B/2) sin(C/2).

mark_split.label: Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula
Apply the product formula and conclude

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the angle condition
steps.margin_note: First mark, and note it is the HALVED condition that is needed — dividing A + B + C = 180° by 2 gives (A+B)/2 = 90° − C/2, which converts sines into cosines and back.
steps.memory_tip: The HALVED condition: dividing by 2 gives (A+B)/2 = 90° − C/2, which swaps sines and cosines.

recall.must_convey: That the angle condition is written down first, in the form the proof will actually use.
accept: write the angle condition first in the form the proof needs
state the given condition and rearrange it
note the angle sum before starting the transformation
modata angle condition rasi, kavalsina form lo pettali
write down the condition on the angles

steps.why: Without the condition the statement is simply false, so it is not preamble — it is the hypothesis the whole proof leans on, and it is used at least twice below.
common_mistakes: Starting the transformation before writing the condition.
Writing the condition but never rearranging it into a usable form.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Three of the eight marks. Three terms will not factorise as they stand, so two of them are combined into a product first. Quote the formula in brackets — the formulas are what the examiner marks.
steps.memory_tip: Convert only TWO of the three terms — converting all three loses track.

recall.must_convey: That one squared sine is turned into 1 − cos² so that a difference of squares appears, leaving the 1 the right-hand side needs.
accept: write sin squared A over two as one minus cos squared A over two so a difference of squares appears
convert one term to get one minus a difference of two squares
replace the first sine squared with one minus cosine squared
modati term ni one minus cos square ga rasi, difference of squares techukovali
turn one of them into one minus cos squared

steps.why: The right-hand side begins with 1, so a 1 has to be manufactured. Converting sin² into 1 − cos² is where it comes from.
common_mistakes: Converting all three terms and losing track.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. This is where the angle condition earns its place: it converts an expression in A and B into one in C, so that every term shares a factor.
steps.memory_tip: cos(90° − C/2) is sin(C/2), not cos(C/2). Watch the sum and difference order in the identity.

recall.must_convey: That cos²A − sin²B = cos(A+B)cos(A−B) is applied, and that cos((A+B)/2) = cos(90° − C/2) = sin(C/2).
accept: use cos squared minus sin squared equals cos of the sum times cos of the difference, then cos of ninety minus C over two is sin C over two
apply the difference of squares identity and convert using the halved angle condition
the cosine of ninety minus C over two becomes sin C over two
cos ninety minus C by two ante sin C by two
convert the half angle using the condition
heard_as: cos A plus B cos A minus B

steps.why: cos(90° − θ) = sin θ is what lets the A and B terms turn into a C term. That conversion is the whole point of halving the condition.
common_mistakes: Applying the identity with the sum and difference swapped.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. The common factor comes out, and the condition is used a SECOND time inside the bracket so that both bracket terms are the same kind of function.
steps.memory_tip: Both bracket terms must be the same kind of function, or no formula applies. There is no 2 to take out.

recall.must_convey: That sin(C/2) is taken out as a common factor and then rewritten inside the bracket as cos((A+B)/2).
accept: take sin C over two common and rewrite the second sin C over two as cos of A plus B over two
factor out sin C over two so the bracket is a difference of cosines
the bracket becomes cos A minus B over two minus cos A plus B over two
sin C by two common teesi, bracket lo cos ga marchali
convert back so both bracket terms are cosines
heard_as: cos A plus B over two

steps.why: The condition is used a second time, in the opposite direction — sine back to cosine — so that the bracket becomes a difference of two cosines the product formula can handle.
common_mistakes: Leaving one bracket term as a sine, so no formula applies.
Taking out 2 sin(C/2) when there is no 2.

steps.label: Apply the product formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. One more sum-or-difference formula turns the bracket into a product, and the identity closes. Write "= R.H.S" so the examiner can see it landed.
steps.memory_tip: Get the ARGUMENT order right or a sign appears, and keep the leading 1.

recall.must_convey: That the difference of the two cosines becomes 2 sin(A/2) sin(B/2), giving 1 − 2 sin(A/2) sin(B/2) sin(C/2).
accept: the difference of cosines gives two sin A over two sin B over two so the answer is one minus two sin A by two sin B by two sin C by two
apply the cosine difference formula to finish
the bracket becomes two sin A by two sin B by two
cos difference formula tho two sin A by two sin B by two vasthundi
the final answer is one minus two sin half A sin half B sin half C

steps.why: Every half-angle question in this chapter ends the same way: a difference of cosines collapses into a product of two sines, supplying the last two factors.
common_mistakes: Getting the order of the arguments wrong and picking up a sign.
